title: Three Treasures 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of finding refuge in one's own embodied experience, rather than relying on external sources or concepts. This involves cultivating awareness of the present moment in the body, which can help develop a sense of connection with others and the world around us. By embracing impermanence and uncertainty, we can find true refuge not in external sources, but in our ability to be present and aware in the midst of life's challenges.

What would a refuge like that feel like?
A refuge where there could be a deep understanding of our own suffering and our own stress and like a real sense of truly coming home and being at ease.
You know, is that possible?
Is it like a place?
Is there anything like that that we could actually rely on?

And it's like the deepest cause of our suffering that we're trying to find some something, right?
Some something outside of me or some object or some teaching or some learning or some psychology or something that we could actually finally rely on some person, right?
Cause of incredible stress in relationships, especially intimate relationships.
Is it possible for our person to be exactly what we need to rely on?
Who cares what they need?
Well, we kind of think we do.

So how could it be, this seems to sort of contradict some of these, of this understanding that in a way we're trying to learn how to rely on nothing or to be like sort of radically okay with there being nothing to rely on.

Something to rely on.
Isn't that great?
You know?
So here we have seemingly some refuge, something to rely on.
And it seems to connect with community.
So maybe the best way for us to take that is a sense of something that's beyond me.
And one thing that's important to notice is the body is mentioned there.
Can I have a chant book?
So it's important to notice that in this first verse it says *Before all beings, immersing body and mind deeply in the way.* So the body is mentioned explicitly.
So this is important.
That we are a body.
That body and mind are together.
We breathe into the body.
We feel the body.
We are the body.

It's an incredibly useful and also somewhat dangerous ability to travel through time and space.
Right?

How could that be our true home?

The body is always just right here which is a great gift to us.

Even or maybe especially when the body is painful when the body is tired when the body is failing when the body is aging the body is teaching us teaching us to be present to really be here to feel the refuge of this deep way that all beings actually walk as human beings from birth to death.

The body encourages us to be in a community that's a real community a real community of real beings and so our embodiment is really what holds us in a space where it's possible to have true refuge, because when we're in the body we're a true person in a way that we aren't really when we're just in our head.

And when our mind is able to encompass this present moment embodied reality, our mind becomes much bigger, and this embodiment and this embracing of just this really can support our mind in opening, and that's what they mean by awakening true mind—the mind that can really feel the bigger and fuller reality than just our own self-concept.
Big mind is what Suzuki Roshi called it.

Out maybe in the middle of the ocean.

One second again, and then we return to community again.

So community has been underlying all of these with the phrase before all beings, but now we explicitly talk about community in the last verse: "I take refuge in Sangha before all beings bringing harmony to everyone, free from hindrance."

Is that through our efforts is there more harmony in our connections, in our relationships, in our communities, in our communication?
Is there more harmony here in the Zendo community?
Is there more harmony in our home lives?
Is there more harmony in our friendships, in our work lives?
So we can look and see, not that we expect to be perfect, or never put a foot wrong, or never say a grumpy word to somebody, or never get confused and screw up.
Of course we will.
We can do an increase in harmony, and we can offer this harmony to everyone, free from hindrance.
And hindrance here is a technical term in Buddhism; it means just what it sounds—some hindrance, some blockage, some barrier.
And the hindrances are habits of mind that prevent us from practicing or cause us to misunderstand practice.
And there are many different lists of hindrances, but the most common list is a list of five, which we've talked about before.
Does anyone remember what the five hindrances are?
Greed and hatred, the first two: greed or desire, hatred or anger, dullness or sleepiness, laziness maybe, and that's paired with its opposite, agitation or restlessness.
So we have two pairs: an emotion desire one, desire and anger, hatred and anger, and an energy one: laziness and dullness or wiredness.
And then those two pairs are under the umbrella of doubt.
Doubt is the fifth one, and doubt is interesting because it's the subtlest of the five.
The three sets, the sixth level of meaning of doubt is that we doubt ourselves and we doubt the practice.
We doubt that we are worthy.
We doubt that this practice will bring real benefit and transformation.
We think, "Oh, you can imagine all kinds of voices, and maybe you know these voices: 'Oh, I'm just going through the motions.
I don't really know what I'm doing.
Probably, this probably isn't really a good version of Zen.
Where's the enlightenment at?' This is like, I guess it's what's in Bellingham, so oh well.
One day I'm going to go to the real place, and then I'll be a real me."
So there's all kinds of doubt.
What's interesting too about doubt is though it's clearly a hindrance, we can also re-imagine doubt as a positive quality.
And Zen is famous for this kind of thing: taking what seems to be a negative quality and turning it around and saying, "Well, wait a minute, maybe doubt is also a great virtue."
And to qualify that in Zen, we talk about great doubt, capital G, capital D, great doubt.
And great doubt is doubt in everything else.
So you meet your doubt of practice, your little doubt of practice, with your doubt in everything else.
Say, "Well, I doubt that we can have a satisfied, happy life from getting a new iPhone.
I tried, and you know, being praised, having happy—you know, all the things that we think at some level or are conditioned to think are going to help us.
We can doubt all that stuff too.
Is that really the real stuff?
Is that it?"
So we can generate a powerful doubt in the validity and completeness of the whole sort of world of samsara.
And that great doubt drives us, you know, encourages us and supports us right back to the cushion, right back to practice.
So we have little doubt and great doubt.
Another way to think about great doubt, which is maybe a little more positive for us, is great curiosity.
Like to really be curious, like, "How does this actually work?"
Like supposedly we kind of think we know how it works, but really?
Do we really know who we are and what we are and who the other people are and how it all works and what's supposed to happen and what's going to happen?
So a kind of great curiosity, a great wondering, a great openness to the mystery of being a human, being a person, being on this planet.
Like what a miracle.
So great doubt is in a way a kind of antidote to ordinary doubt, to little doubt, but it's also a great sort of healing in itself.
And again, we do all this with support.
We do all this with support.
And it's really incredible if you watch your mind, even over the course of seeing these words or listening to these words in your case, the mind comes so quickly back to, "Okay, what do I got to do?
It's up to me.
It's only me.
I'm the only one."
Right?
We all kind of think that.
It's just me.
I mean, I kind of admit that you other people might be here, maybe, just projections of my own mind, you know?
So we really need to work with the little voice that says, "It's just me.
It's my problem.
It's my fault.
It's my responsibility."
It is, I suppose.
But that view is not going to allow us to touch the refuge of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Again, we need all beings.
So we need the teacher.
We need our peers.
We need our elders.
We need our biological family.
Even if our relationship with them has been a great trouble, it would be great.
And we need to be able to have conversations about what really matters.
To notice how often we use our creative energy and our speaking voice to talk about things that aren't important, to reassure ourselves, to pass the time, to fill the space.
So in taking refuge in Sangha, we can practice having real conversations.
And so that's partly why we have the interview room practice and Zen practice.

It would be great if we used that all the more to go to practice discussion with the teachers besides me, who are qualified to offer that, to come to Dokusan regularly, to just show up in those meetings.
You have no idea what you're going to say, just to show up in order to practice taking refuge.
Just practice taking refuge.
I'm here to be with you and practice harmony, to practice entering, to practice being in body and mind, to practice awakening, and to see what happens.
And maybe something happens that's obvious to our mind, or might not be obvious to our mind.
And so that's another way to look at a practice of taking refuge in Sangha.
And what's also challenging about these kind of teachings is the only way to talk about these teachings is to put them into words, right?
And so I've attempted to offer a bunch of words, and it's a little bit stressful because I was having trouble reading my notes.
It's funny, someone just asked me for tips about how to give dharma talks, and so I feel like it's the most awkward talk I've given in years, just because of my little gadget here.
I forgot my printout.
But we're limited by our words, right?
This taking refuge is something that we can point to with these words, with these chants, that we use words in order to bring them out into our felt experience.
But this is really a feeling.
It's really a feeling that we're cultivating, a feeling in the body, a feeling in the heart, a feeling that there's something that we can deeply trust.
And it's not the same stuff that we're always trying to kind of grab onto and hold tight or push away from.
It's fluid, and it's hard to quite put our finger on, or stand on.
Which brings me back one last time to the Prajnaparamita teachings, that wonderful part we talked about where Subhuti, I think, is saying, "How do bodhisattvas stand in perfect wisdom?
Just like how do we actually enter refuge?
How do the bodhisattvas stand in perfect wisdom?"
It's by seeing that there's nowhere to stand.
That's how they stand in perfect wisdom.
So this refuge has that quality too.

We can enter this refuge when we let go of refuge, when we allow ourselves to just be fully ourselves, through our limitations, through our small doubt, through our great doubt, through community, through connection, through our own suffering, and through those little glimmers that happen all the time that freedom is right here as well.
So that's a few words about taking refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Sangha before all beings.
